questions.prompt: How does Copy-on-Write (COW) optimize Swift collections?

options.text: It writes all modified collections to disk automatically.
options.explanation: COW manages memory storage buffers, not disk persistence.

options.text: It shares storage across copies until a mutation happens.
options.explanation: Right. Memory is only duplicated when one of the copies is modified.

options.explanation: Mutations are still allowed; COW simply delays buffer duplication.

questions.prompt: Compare Array, Set, and Dictionary in Swift. Explain when you should choose each collection type. Answer in 2–4 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Defines Array as ordered with integer index and duplicate support
Defines Set as unordered unique elements with fast membership checks
Defines Dictionary as key-value pairs with unique Hashable keys

questions.modelAnswer: An Array is an ordered collection accessed by integer index, ideal when element order matters or duplicates are allowed. A Set is an unordered collection of unique elements, ideal for deduplication and fast O(1) membership testing. A Dictionary stores key-value pairs, ideal for looking up values by unique identifiers like user IDs or configuration names.

sources.title: The Swift Programming Language: Collection Types

questions.prompt: What happens when you access an out-of-bounds array index? How does this differ from reading a missing dictionary key? Answer in 2–4 sentences.

rubric.criterion: States that reading an out-of-bounds array index causes a fatal runtime crash
States that looking up a missing key in a dictionary returns nil safely
Explains that array indices represent contiguous memory slots while dictionary keys represent optional lookups

questions.modelAnswer: Reading an out-of-bounds index on an array causes an immediate fatal runtime crash because Swift assumes indexed access into contiguous memory must be valid. In contrast, subscripting a dictionary with a missing key returns nil safely inside an optional. Because keys are frequently missing in dynamic applications, dictionaries handle absent entries gracefully without terminating the program.

sources.title: The Swift Programming Language: Collection Types

questions.prompt: Why must elements stored in a Set or keys used in a Dictionary conform to the Hashable protocol? Answer in 2–4 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that Hashable produces an integer hash value used to find hash table buckets
States that hash tables enable constant time O(1) lookups and insertions
Mentions that Hashable inherits from Equatable to resolve hash collisions

questions.modelAnswer: Types stored in a Set or used as Dictionary keys must conform to Hashable so the collection can compute an integer hash value. This hash value determines which internal hash bucket stores the element, enabling amortized O(1) lookup and insertion. Because Hashable inherits from Equatable, the collection can also compare items directly when multiple elements produce the same hash value.

sources.title: The Swift Programming Language: Collection Types

questions.prompt: How does the default subscript syntax dictionary[key, default: value] work, and why is it useful when counting occurrences? Answer in 2–4 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that it returns the existing value or the default fallback if the key is missing
Explains that it produces a non-optional value allowing in-place mutation like += 1
Contrasts with manual optional unwrapping which requires extra lines of code

questions.modelAnswer: The default subscript syntax retrieves the existing value for a key. If the key is missing, it provides the fallback value. Because it returns a non-optional mutable value, developers can write expressions like counts[word, default: 0] += 1 in a single line. This eliminates cumbersome manual optional binding and simplifies aggregation algorithms.

sources.title: The Swift Programming Language: Collection Types

questions.prompt: Explain how Copy-on-Write (COW) works for Swift collections and why it balances safety with performance. Answer in 2–4 sentences.

rubric.criterion: States that Swift collections are value types that share storage buffers until modified
Explains that a new memory copy is only created when a write mutation occurs
Highlights that this prevents expensive redundant copying when passing collections to functions

questions.modelAnswer: All standard Swift collections are value types implemented as structs, providing independent behavior without unexpected side effects. To avoid expensive memory copies, Swift uses Copy-on-Write to share the underlying storage buffer among copies as long as they are read-only. When a copy mutates its content, Swift creates a separate memory buffer, keeping value safety while maintaining excellent performance.
